strengths: The paper addresses a relevant practical question: how compression affects reasoning models beyond perplexity and basic language understanding.
The evaluation covers mathematical, logical, temporal, and knowledge-intensive multihop tasks, including three quantization levels and seven pruning levels for each of two distilled models.

The sparsity sweeps provide useful descriptive evidence of task-dependent degradation: AIME performance deteriorates earlier than temporal reasoning, while highly pruned models exhibit repetitive generation.
weaknesses: The reported results contain a serious internal inconsistency. Tables 2–3 give unpruned R1-Distill-Qwen 1% EM on 100 MuSiQue questions, implying one correct answer. Table 4 reports 16.7% EM in both disjoint 30-question subsets, implying approximately ten correct answers across those subsets alone. Table 5 similarly implies eight correct answers. Related inconsistencies affect pruned Qwen rows. These discrepancies require reconciliation before the findings can be trusted.

The central claim that parameter count affects knowledge more than reasoning is not isolated experimentally. R1, Llama-70B, and Qwen-32B differ in architecture, pretraining, and training history as well as size. Closed-book MuSiQue jointly measures factual recall and reasoning, so its scores cannot disentangle these capabilities. Controlled size comparisons, factual subquestion evaluation, and supplied-evidence conditions are needed to support the compression recommendations.

The output-length analysis establishes an association, not that reducing verbosity improves reasoning. Shortest and longest outputs correspond to different questions; harder questions can independently produce longer responses and lower accuracy. The recommendation requires within-question comparisons or controlled generation-budget interventions. Counting words also provides only a crude proxy for tokens and does not measure comparable compute across architectures.

Statistical support is inadequate for the reported rankings. Every benchmark receives one stochastic pass, with only 30 AIME questions and 100 sampled MuSiQue questions, and no uncertainty estimates or repeated trials. The claimed AIME improvement from 73.3% to 76.7% is just one additional correct answer; the extreme-length AIME subsets contain only six or nine questions.

The full-model baseline uses an external API, whereas compressed models run locally on different inference systems. The paper reports repeatedly retrying empty API responses but does not document failure rates, retry limits, or precise API checkpoint identity. This weakens attribution of differences to compression, and the proposed explanation involving security mechanisms is speculative.

The comparison does not establish which compression method offers the best practical tradeoff. It omits model storage, peak memory, latency, and comparisons at matched resource budgets. Quantizing a 671B model and distilling to 32B or 70B produce substantially different deployment requirements; unstructured sparsity also does not automatically translate into inference savings.

The empirical contribution is narrow relative to its broad recommendations: one teacher family, one quantization approach, two existing distilled checkpoints, and one pruning algorithm, without alternative compression baselines or undistilled student controls. Reproducibility is further limited by missing prompt templates, answer-extraction rules, MuSiQue sample identifiers, pruning calibration details, software versions, and evaluation code. Together with the unsupported central interpretations, this falls below the evidentiary standard for a top-tier conference.

strengths: Addresses a relevant practical question: how compression affects reasoning models across mathematical, logical, temporal, and knowledge-intensive tasks.
Evaluates three compression paradigms and seven pruning sparsity levels on two distilled models, providing useful descriptive evidence of task-dependent degradation.
Reports accuracy, answer-quality metrics, and output-length analyses, with qualitative examples illustrating repetition at high sparsity.
weaknesses: The reported results contain a serious internal inconsistency. Tables 2–3 give unpruned R1-Distill-Qwen 1% MuSiQue EM on 100 questions, implying one correct answer. Table 4 reports 16.7% EM in both disjoint 30-question length subsets, implying ten correct answers. Table 5 likewise implies eight correct answers. These cannot describe the stated single evaluation run and undermine confidence in the findings.

The central claim that parameter count affects knowledge more than reasoning is not isolated experimentally. Comparing Qwen-32B, Llama-70B, and R1 confounds size with architecture, pretraining, and distillation. Closed-book MuSiQue also mixes factual recall with multihop reasoning. Within-family size comparisons and matched evaluations with and without supporting facts are needed.

The recommendation to shorten reasoning overinterprets an observational correlation. Difficult questions can cause both longer responses and more errors; comparing different questions grouped by realized output length does not show that reducing verbosity improves accuracy. Controlled interventions on reasoning length are missing.

Statistical support is weak: evaluation uses one stochastic generation per question, only 30 AIME questions, and 100 sampled MuSiQue questions, without uncertainty estimates or repeated runs. The apparent AIME improvement from 73.3% to 76.7% is just one additional correct answer; the extreme length subsets contain only six or nine questions.

Compression comparisons do not establish practical tradeoffs. There are no matched memory budgets, model-size measurements, latency measurements, or resource–accuracy curves. Quantization is applied to the 671B teacher while pruning is applied to distilled students. Counting words as tokens is also an inadequate measure of computational cost across these architectures.

Reproducibility and baseline control are insufficient. The paper omits prompt templates, answer-extraction procedures, MuSiQue sample identifiers, pruning calibration details, and implementation versions. The full-model baseline uses an API with repeated attempts after empty responses, whereas compressed models run locally; the retry protocol and possible effects are not quantified.

The contribution remains a limited benchmark application of existing checkpoints and SparseGPT. Only one quantization approach and one pruning method are tested, Temporal performance is largely saturated, and broader recommendations about compression methods exceed the experimental coverage. The useful descriptive results do not compensate for the unresolved reporting and validity issues.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant question: how compression affects complex reasoning rather than only perplexity or basic language tasks.
The evaluation spans mathematical, logical, temporal, and knowledge-intensive reasoning, with three quantization levels and a substantial pruning sweep across two distilled models.
The reported preservation of performance under aggressive quantization and the task-dependent degradation under pruning provide potentially useful empirical observations.
weaknesses: The reported results contain a serious internal inconsistency. Tables 2–3 give unpruned R1-Distill-Qwen 1% MuSiQue EM on 100 questions, meaning one correct answer. Table 4 reports 16.7% EM in both the shortest and longest 30% subsets, implying approximately five correct answers in each disjoint subset. These results cannot describe the same evaluation. Similar contradictions occur for the 30%-pruned Qwen model and in Table 5. This undermines confidence in the knowledge and response-length analyses.

The central claim that parameter count affects knowledge more than reasoning is not isolated experimentally. R1, Llama-70B, and Qwen-32B differ in architecture, pretraining, and training history as well as size. Closed-book MuSiQue jointly measures factual availability and multihop reasoning. Matched model families, factual-recall controls, and evaluation with supplied supporting evidence are needed to separate these effects.

The response-length analysis establishes an association, not that reducing verbosity improves reasoning. Short and long responses answer different questions, so difficulty and model uncertainty are major confounders. Controlled generation budgets or repeated responses to the same questions are needed to support the recommendation.

Statistical support is weak: each benchmark receives only one stochastic pass, AIME contains 30 questions, and MuSiQue uses only 100 sampled questions. No uncertainty estimates or repeated runs are reported. The apparent AIME improvement from 73.3% to 76.7% is just one additional correct answer; the extreme-length AIME subsets contain only six or nine questions.

Compression recommendations lack comparable resource budgets. The study measures neither actual memory/storage savings nor latency or throughput, and compares a quantized 671B MoE with much smaller dense students. Counting words as tokens also provides only a rough output-length measure, not comparable computational cost across these architectures.

Coverage and novelty are limited for a top-tier benchmark contribution: the study evaluates existing checkpoints and one pruning method within the R1 ecosystem, without alternative quantization/pruning baselines or another independently trained reasoning model. Temporal reasoning is almost saturated, further limiting discrimination.

Reproducibility and baseline control are insufficient. Exact prompts, answer-extraction procedures, SparseGPT calibration data and settings, sampling seeds, and implementation versions are not adequately documented. The original R1 is evaluated through an API with repeated attempts after empty responses, while compressed models run locally; the retry policy and its effects are not quantified.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important question: how compression affects reasoning models beyond conventional perplexity evaluations. It benchmarks multiple quantizers, four distilled model sizes, and a range of pruning sparsities across four tasks.

The module-level analysis generates an actionable hypothesis. Preserving the final-layer MLP in 16-bit improves Llama-8B’s average accuracy from 46.0 to 52.57 under otherwise 3-bit AWQ, providing useful preliminary evidence for selective precision allocation.
The pruning sweep and single-module quantization experiments offer more diagnostic evidence than aggregate benchmark comparisons alone. Most main-table configurations are evaluated over three runs.
weaknesses: The central causal interpretation is insufficiently justified. The proposed score measures a first-order change in token cross-entropy along a behavior-associated activation direction; it does not establish that a module causally implements that reasoning behavior. Contrasting labeled spans against entire sequences, including prompts and positive examples, can capture token identity or position. No direct activation-patching validation or behavior-specific intervention establishes the claimed causal relationship. Furthermore, a decrease in normalized relative importance need not indicate diminished absolute contribution, making the interpretation of importance shifts as compression damage unreliable.

The conclusion that parameter count affects knowledge more than reasoning is confounded. Comparing Llama-70B with Qwen-32B changes pretraining, architecture, and specialization alongside size. Closed-book MuSiQue combines factual recall, multihop reasoning, and answer generation, so its score does not isolate memorization. Its 100-question sample and near-floor performance for several models further weaken this inference. Matched within-family comparisons and separate recall and reasoning controls are needed before recommending against distillation or pruning for knowledge-intensive tasks.

The validation of module importance is narrow and partly contradicts the proposed ranking. Table 3 tests only five modules in Llama-8B. The lowest-ranked up projection, 1_up, produces almost as much average degradation as the highest-ranked 32_up and substantially greater AIME degradation. There is no systematic rank-versus-intervention correlation, control for quantization-error magnitude, or corresponding intervention validation on Qwen. Comparing distilled models with their backbones also cannot establish that pretrained weights play little role in reasoning.

The headline mixed-precision result lacks appropriate controls. Table 4 covers only Llama-8B with AWQ, without equal-memory random-module protection, other-layer protection, or conventional sensitivity-based allocation. Keeping approximately 2% of weights at 16-bit increases nominal average precision from 3 to about 3.26 bits, so comparisons against uniformly 3-bit baselines do not establish superiority at a matched storage budget. The gate-projection claim is not directly validated, and generalization across quantizers and model families remains untested.

Statistical support is limited: AIME contains only 30 questions, MuSiQue only 100, and R1 plus its dynamically quantized variants receive one run. No confidence intervals or run-level dispersion are reported. Consequently, small differences and precise collapse thresholds are uncertain. Cross-paradigm comparisons also use substantially different compression budgets, limiting conclusions about which strategy is best.

Reproducibility and positioning need improvement. The interpretation dataset, annotation prompts and validation, calibration configurations, seeds, and detailed attribution implementation are insufficiently specified; the code footnote is incomplete. The methodological novelty largely combines existing difference-of-means and attribution techniques at module granularity, while comparisons against simpler importance measures and established mixed-precision selection approaches are missing.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant practical question: how compression affects reasoning models. Its benchmarking spans several quantization methods, distilled model sizes, pruning levels, and four tasks.

The selective protection experiment provides a promising empirical result: retaining final-layer MLP weights in full precision improves Llama-8B’s average accuracy from 46.0 to 52.57, a gain of 6.57 percentage points.
The component-level analysis and single-component quantization experiments go beyond aggregate benchmarking and identify potentially useful directions for compression research.
weaknesses: The central causal interpretation is insufficiently justified. The proposed score measures a first-order change in token cross-entropy along a constructed activation direction; this does not establish that a component causally implements a particular reasoning behavior. Behavior-specific activation interventions, matched non-reasoning controls, and validation of GPT-4o’s behavior annotations are missing. Furthermore, a decrease in normalized relative importance can arise because other components increase, without any loss of the component’s capability. Discarding increases does not resolve this ambiguity.

The conclusion that parameter count affects knowledge more than reasoning is confounded. Comparisons between Llama and Qwen also change pretraining data, architecture, and specialization. Closed-book MuSiQue mixes factual recall with multihop reasoning and uses only 100 questions, with near-floor performance for several models. The pruning results are also mixed: Qwen’s AIME accuracy falls sharply at 50% sparsity while its already-low MuSiQue scores do not consistently decline. These experiments cannot support the broad recommendation against pruning and distillation for knowledge-intensive tasks.

The validation of the importance ranking is limited and contains substantial counterevidence. Table 3 tests only five components in one model. The lowest-ranked up projection, 1_up, produces almost as much average degradation as the highest-ranked 32_up and substantially worse AIME accuracy. A systematic correlation between predicted importance and intervention effects, with uncertainty estimates and controls for quantization error, is needed.

The claimed superiority of the protection strategy lacks appropriate controls. Table 4 evaluates only Llama-8B with 3-bit AWQ, despite broader claims across model families and quantizers. There are no equal-memory comparisons against random module protection, protecting other layers, or conventional sensitivity-based selection. Keeping approximately 2% of weights at 16 bits increases the precision budget, so comparisons with uniformly 3-bit baselines do not isolate the value of the proposed interpretation method.

The distillation analysis compares a fine-tuned student with its pretrained backbone, rather than isolating information retained or lost relative to the teacher. Similarity between importance and importance-shift heatmaps does not establish that pretrained weights play little role in reasoning, as claimed in Section 4.3.

Statistical support is weak for several headline comparisons. AIME contains only 30 problems; full R1, dynamically quantized R1, and the sparsity sweep use single sampled runs. Other results average three runs without reporting dispersion or confidence intervals. Temporal accuracy is often saturated. Consequently, small differences and precise collapse-point claims are not robustly established.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript does not adequately specify the interpretation dataset and sample counts, annotation prompts and validation, calibration configurations, or evaluation prompts. The code-availability footnote is unfinished. Combined with the unresolved methodological issues, the evidence is insufficient for acceptance at a top-tier conference.

strengths: Addresses a relevant practical problem: preserving reasoning capabilities under compression. The evaluation covers several quantizers, four distilled model sizes, pruning sparsity sweeps, and four reasoning benchmarks.
Combines performance benchmarking with module-level attribution and intervention experiments, providing more insight than accuracy comparisons alone.

The final-layer protection result is promising: retaining approximately 2% of weights in full precision improves Llama-8B’s average accuracy from 46.0 to 52.57. Selective quantization also demonstrates substantial sensitivity to the final-layer up projection.
weaknesses: The mechanistic analysis does not establish the claimed causal relationships. Directional gradients of token cross-entropy measure local sensitivity, which need not identify components responsible for reasoning behaviors. Behavior spans are contrasted with entire sequences, including prompts, without controls for token identity or position. Moreover, decreases in normalized relative importance need not imply lost capability; discarding increases makes this interpretation particularly incomplete.

Validation of the importance ranking is limited to five components in one model and contains a substantial counterexample. In Table 3, the lowest-ranked up projection, 1_up, produces an average accuracy of 50.5, nearly as damaging as the highest-ranked 32_up at 48.9, and causes the largest AIME degradation. Broader intervention coverage, quantitative rank correlations, and behavior-specific validation are needed.

The conclusion that parameter count affects knowledge more than reasoning is confounded by architecture, pretraining, specialization, and task difficulty. Closed-book MuSiQue mixes retrieval and reasoning and uses only 100 questions, with near-floor scores for several models. Comparing different student backbones does not isolate parameter count or knowledge loss caused by distillation. Likewise, attribution shifts after fine-tuning do not establish that pretrained weights play little role in reasoning.

The mixed-precision improvement is demonstrated only for 3-bit AWQ on Llama-8B. There are no equal-budget random-module, alternative-layer, or established sensitivity-based protection baselines, nor an intervention validating the middle-layer gate-projection claim. Keeping 2% of weights at 16 bits raises nominal average precision to approximately 3.26 bits, so comparisons against uniform 3-bit methods do not establish superiority at equal storage cost.

Statistical support is insufficient for several comparisons. AIME contains only 30 problems; full R1, dynamic quantization, and pruning sweeps use single passes, while other results average three runs without uncertainty estimates. Temporal accuracy is often saturated. The apparent AIME advantage of 2.51-bit R1 over full R1 is just one additional correct answer.

Compression strategies are compared across different model sizes, architectures, and resource budgets without memory or compute trade-off curves. Pruning is represented by one method, and distillation uses existing checkpoints. These experiments support observations about selected configurations more strongly than general recommendations about compression paradigms.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the interpretation-code footnote is unfinished, and the manuscript does not adequately specify the interpretation corpus and sample counts, GPT-4o annotation prompts and validation, held-out evaluation separation, or key quantization and pruning calibration settings. Overall, the useful empirical observations do not yet support the paper’s broad causal and generalization claims at a top-tier acceptance standard.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical question: how compression affects reasoning models. Its benchmarking spans several model sizes, three compression paradigms, and mathematical, logical, temporal, and knowledge-intensive tasks.

The module-level analysis produces a potentially useful observation about final-layer MLP sensitivity. Selective quantization experiments provide supporting evidence beyond heatmap inspection, including additional checks on Qwen in Appendix N.
Protecting the final-layer MLP improves Llama-8B’s average accuracy from 46.0 to 52.57 under 3-bit AWQ. The appendices also extend the analysis to pruning and a non-R1 distilled model.
weaknesses: The mechanistic analysis does not establish the claimed fine-grained causal relationships with reasoning behaviors. The proposed score measures local cross-entropy sensitivity along a behavior-associated activation direction; this can reflect lexical predictability or general language modeling rather than reasoning. The negative set includes all outputs, including positive examples, and no matched non-reasoning controls or direct behavior-specific activation interventions are provided. Selective weight quantization establishes component sensitivity, but does not validate the four proposed behavioral interpretations.

Decreases in normalized importance are treated as evidence that a module’s reasoning capability has been damaged. However, relative importance can decrease solely because another module’s score increases, even when its own absolute score is unchanged. Appendix H displays increases and net changes but does not resolve this identification problem. Likewise, comparing a distilled model with its backbone cannot justify the strong claim that the original backbone weights play little role in shaping reasoning.

The central conclusion that parameter count affects knowledge more than reasoning is inadequately controlled. Comparing Llama-70B with Qwen-32B confounds size with pretraining, architecture, and knowledge coverage. Closed-book multihop QA combines retrieval, reasoning, and answer production; the RAG experiments change information availability without isolating these factors. Near-zero MuSiQue scores for small models also create floor effects, so unchanged scores after quantization provide weak evidence of knowledge preservation.

The mixed-precision result lacks essential controls for the claimed superiority over existing methods. Retaining approximately 2% of weights in 16-bit increases the storage budget relative to uniform 3-bit baselines. There are no equal-budget comparisons, random-module protection controls, or comparisons against simple activation- or quantization-error-based selection. The protection experiment is restricted to one model and one quantizer, and does not separately validate the proposed importance of middle-layer gate projections.

Statistical support is insufficient for several conclusions. AIME contains only 30 questions and MuSiQue only 100; full R1, dynamically quantized models, and several diagnostic experiments use single passes. Most other results report three-pass averages without uncertainty estimates. The annotation validation uses only ten samples per behavior, sampled with replacement, and assigns perfect scores to outputs with no detected behavior. It therefore does not establish annotation recall or stability of the resulting module rankings.

The benchmarking is useful descriptively but does not support general recommendations among compression paradigms: model architectures, sizes, calibration, and inference platforms differ, and comparisons do not match memory or compute budgets. Reproducibility is also incomplete: calibration data and settings, sampled evaluation IDs, annotation prompts, and implementation versions are insufficiently specified. Overall, the promising empirical observation does not yet compensate for the unresolved controls and overextended central claims.

strengths: Addresses a relevant practical question through a reasonably broad benchmark of quantization, pruning, and distilled reasoning models across four tasks.
Combines module-level attribution with selective quantization interventions. The sensitivity of the final-layer MLP is an interesting empirical observation with potential value for compression.

Protecting the final-layer MLP improves Llama-8B average accuracy from 46.0 to 52.57. Appendices provide additional sparsity sweeps, annotation checks, and exploratory evidence on a non-R1 distilled model.
weaknesses: The central knowledge-versus-reasoning conclusion is not adequately isolated. Comparisons across Llama, Qwen, and R1 confound parameter count with architecture, pretraining data, and specialization. Closed-book MuSiQue requires both knowledge and reasoning, and its near-zero scores for smaller models create floor effects. The additional RAG experiment improves EM only to 2% and does not establish that reasoning remains intact while knowledge is lost.

The mechanistic claims exceed the validation. A steering-vector/gradient dot product measures local sensitivity of token cross-entropy, not necessarily a causal contribution to a reasoning behavior. Missing controls include unrelated token spans, generic language-model loss, and direct behavior-specific activation interventions. Normalized importance can decrease because other modules increase, so decreased relative importance does not itself establish damage from compression.

The selective protection experiment lacks equal-budget controls. Retaining about 2% of weights at 16 bits increases the nominal average precision from 3 to approximately 3.26 bits, yet comparisons are against ordinary 3-bit methods. Random-module protection, alternative layer protection, and established sensitivity-based allocation are needed to demonstrate the attribution method's added value. The reported gain is 6.57 percentage points on one model and one quantization setup; broader superiority claims are premature.

Statistical support is weak for several central results. AIME contains only 30 questions and MuSiQue only 100; key intervention and sparsity tables lack uncertainty estimates, while some evaluations use a single pass. In Table 3, the lowest-ranked first-layer up projection nearly matches the top-ranked module's average degradation and causes a larger AIME drop. Appendix N offers further examples but does not establish reliable ranking performance across modules.

The distillation interpretation overreaches. Comparing a student with its pretrained backbone measures changes after fine-tuning, rather than directly tracing compression from the teacher. Similar importance patterns do not show that original pretrained weights play little role in reasoning. Likewise, one additional distilled Qwen model provides limited evidence for generalization across non-R1 model families.

Reproducibility and practical comparisons remain incomplete. The manuscript omits several calibration, quantization, annotation, and sampling details needed to reproduce the analysis. Compression strategies are compared at different resource budgets without a matched memory-quality analysis. Together with the unresolved causal and experimental issues, this leaves the contribution below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical question: how compression affects reasoning models. Its benchmark covers several model sizes, three compression paradigms, and mathematical, logical, temporal, and knowledge-intensive tasks.

The final-layer MLP finding is promising and actionable. Selective quantization provides some intervention-based evidence, and protecting the final-layer MLP improves average accuracy from 46.0 to 52.57 in Table 4.
The appendices strengthen the empirical investigation through sparsity sweeps, additional selective-quantization experiments, annotation checks, and an initial extension to a non-R1 distilled model.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic claims exceed what the importance metric establishes. A directional derivative of cross-entropy on annotated text measures local sensitivity, not necessarily causal importance for the corresponding reasoning behavior. Differences in linguistic content, activation scale, and proximity to the output could influence the scores. The selective-quantization experiments measure overall accuracy rather than behavior-specific effects, and lack comparisons against simpler importance measures.

Decreases in normalized importance do not establish that a component's reasoning capability has diminished: its relative score can decrease solely because another component's score increases. Appendix H provides additional visualizations but does not resolve this conceptual problem. Similarly, comparing a distilled model with its pretrained backbone measures changes associated with fine-tuning; it does not isolate compression from the teacher or justify claiming that original weights play little role.

The claim that parameter count affects knowledge more than reasoning is insufficiently controlled. Comparisons between Llama-70B and Qwen-32B confound size with pretraining, architecture, and specialization. Closed-book MuSiQue also requires reasoning, so it is not an isolated memorization test. The RAG experiment changes access to information and does not compare model sizes under matched evidence. The non-R1 experiment preserves an already low 4% EM score, providing limited additional support.

The proposed protection strategy lacks budget-matched controls. Keeping approximately 2% of weights at 16-bit raises nominal average precision from 3 to roughly 3.26 bits, excluding metadata. Comparisons should include equally sized random or alternative protected modules and competitive mixed-precision allocations. The demonstrated improvement is confined to one model and one quantizer; heatmap similarities elsewhere do not establish equivalent practical gains.

Statistical support is weak for several headline conclusions. AIME contains only 30 questions and MuSiQue uses 100 sampled questions. Some central results use single runs, and performance tables lack uncertainty estimates. Three-run averages elsewhere do not establish the reliability of differences or precise collapse thresholds. In Table 3, the lowest-ranked first-layer up projection damages AIME more than the highest-ranked final-layer projection; the additional experiments help, but do not justify attributing this discrepancy to randomness without repeated measurements.

Compression comparisons are not matched for memory or compute, limiting claims that one strategy is preferable. Reproducibility is also incomplete: Appendix D gives decoding settings and frameworks but omits important calibration specifications, quantization settings, seeds, and interpretation implementation details. Overall, the useful exploratory observations do not yet support the broad causal and state-of-the-art claims required for acceptance.
